newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN-OAU envoy named to tackle Central Africa crises.
newsitem.headline: UN-OAU envoy named to tackle Central Africa crises.

text.p: Algerian diplomat Mohammed Sahnoun, who once headed the U.N. operation in Somalia, was named on Wednesday to tackle linked crises that threaten the stability of Central Africa's Great Lakes region.

Secretary-General Kofi Annan gave details of the appointment in a letter to the Security Council saying Sahnoun would serve as special representative of both the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity (OAU).
He will be based in Nairobi, Kenya, but will travel extensively throughout the region, which includes Rwanda, Burundi and Zaire.

Between 500,000 and a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed in genocidal massacres in Rwanda in 1994. Hundreds of thousands of refugees fled, mainly to neighbouring Zaire, including many Hutus who feared retribution after Tutsis wrested power from Hutu hardliners.
In Burundi, more than 150,000 people have been killed in civil war and massacres since 1993 when the country's first Hutu president was murdered in an attempted army coup.
In eastern Zaire, where hundreds of thousands of refugees remain, fighting between Tutsi-led rebels and government troops is threatening a break-up of the sprawling, mineral-rich country.

Sahnoun, who has been Algeria's ambassador to the United Nations, the United States, Germany and France, headed the U.N. operation in Somalia for about six months in 1992 until a row with then-Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
He was rebuked and fired by Boutros-Ghali, whom Annan succeeded on Jan. 1, for saying publicly that the United Nations came too late to save many of the millions of Somalis then facing starvation.
Sahnoun also served as deputy secretary-general of the Arab League in 1973 and from 1964 to 1973 was deputy secretary-general of the OAU.

His daunting mandate in the Great Lakes region, as spelled out by Annan, will be to promote the peaceful settlement of the various conflicts, especially in eastern Zaire and Burundi at first, and to prepare an international conference on peace, security and development in the entire region.
He will use his good offices to "help preserve the unity and territorial integrity of Zaire and...help restore that country's national institutions."
Sahnoun will also direct other U.N. political activities in the region and ensure coordination of U.N. aid programmes.

Annan, who made the appointment in agreement with OAU Secretary-General Salim Salim of Tanzania, said Sahnoun would need an aircraft, communications and other logistical support to enable him to travel extensively.
He will eventually establish sub-offices in Bujumbura, Kigali and Kinshasa, the capitals of Burundi, Rwanda and Zaire, and possibly in other centres.
Annan told the Security Council that support would be needed for Sahnoun's mission as well as financial contributions for humanitarian activities in the region.
